name: Mirtazapine
sections: White to creamy-white crystalline powder; melting point 114–116 °C; racemic mixture.
First synthesised at Organon and published in 1989; a tetracyclic piperazino-azepine structurally related to mianserin. First approval/introduction: Netherlands 1994; US FDA 1996 (Organon).

Blocks presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic auto- and heteroreceptors, increasing release of norepinephrine and serotonin; blocks 5-HT2 and 5-HT3 receptors so serotonergic effect is channelled through 5-HT1A. Potent H1 antagonism gives sedation and appetite stimulation. Receptor / target profile: Potent antagonist of alpha-2A/2B/2C adrenoceptors, 5-HT2A, 5-HT2C, 5-HT3 and H1 receptors (H1 Ki 0.14–1.6 nM); does not inhibit monoamine reuptake.
Summary: Bioavailability ~50%; Tmax ~2 h. ~85% protein bound. Metabolised by CYP2D6, CYP1A2 and CYP3A4. Half-life 20–40 h.
Major depressive disorder, especially with insomnia, anxiety or poor appetite
Off-label: insomnia, appetite stimulation, anxiety disorders
Start 15 mg once daily at bedtime; increase up to 45 mg/day as needed (dose changes at ≥1–2 week intervals)
7.5 mg used for elderly or when sedation is the main target
Place MD tablet on the tongue to disperse; swallow with or without water
Reduce dose in hepatic or renal impairment
Dose to be individualised by the treating physician according to clinical response and tolerability.

With or without food; avoid alcohol (additive sedation).
CBC if fever/sore throat (agranulocytosis); weight; lipids; LFTs.
Disorientation, prolonged sedation, tachycardia, mild hypertension/hypotension. Supportive care.
Cipriani et al., Lancet 2018 – mirtazapine among the more efficacious antidepressants.
HTA-SADD (Banerjee et al., Lancet 2011) – no benefit over placebo for depression in dementia.
Report sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers immediately
Store below 30°C in a dry place, protected from light and moisture. Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the expiry date.
